Direct project signals are modest at 15 GitHub stars, and the API intentionally stops before formatting, conversion, or manipulation, leaving those jobs to companion packages or a broader color library.

patterns.title: Parse short and long hexadecimal colors
patterns.note: Four-digit and eight-digit hex treat the last component as alpha. The returned alpha is a 0 through 1 number, not the original byte.

patterns.title: Guard the null result before destructuring
patterns.note: Invalid syntax, unsupported keywords, and non-string values return null. The parser does not throw its own validation error.

patterns.title: Trim a form value before parsing
patterns.note: The test suite expects ' transparent' and 'transparent ' to fail. Trim only when surrounding whitespace is acceptable in your input contract.

patterns.title: Parse modern RGB syntax with alpha
patterns.snippet:
const color = parseCssColor('rgb(255 0 153 / 20%)');
// { type: 'rgb', values: [255, 0, 153], alpha: 0.2 }
patterns.note: All three RGB channels must use numbers or all three must use percentages. Mixed numeric and percentage channels return null.

patterns.title: Convert percentage RGB channels to bytes
patterns.snippet:
const color = parseCssColor('rgb(41.2% 69.88% 96.64%)');
// { type: 'rgb', values: [105, 178, 246], alpha: 1 }
patterns.note: Percentage channels are multiplied by 255 and rounded to integers. This can lose the original percentage precision.

patterns.title: Parse HSL hue units
patterns.note: Radians and turns are converted to degrees. HSL results are not converted to RGB, so branch on type downstream.

patterns.title: Parse a named CSS color
patterns.snippet:
const color = parseCssColor('RebeccaPurple');
// { type: 'rgb', values: [102, 51, 153], alpha: 1 }
patterns.note: Named-color lookup is case-insensitive and comes from color-name. System colors and misspelled names return null.

patterns.title: Handle the transparent keyword
patterns.snippet:
const color = parseCssColor('transparent');
// { type: 'rgb', values: [0, 0, 0], alpha: 0 }
patterns.note: transparent is represented as transparent black. Do not preserve its RGB channels as meaningful color information when alpha is zero.

patterns.title: Reject CSS-wide and context-dependent values
patterns.note: The package supports literal hex, RGB, HSL, named colors, and transparent only. It cannot resolve values that depend on CSS context.

patterns.title: Account for clamped channel values
patterns.snippet:
const color = parseCssColor('rgb(500 -100 12.6 / 200%)');
// { type: 'rgb', values: [255, 0, 13], alpha: 1 }
patterns.note: Out-of-range numeric channels are clamped and RGB fractions are rounded. If out-of-range input must be invalid, validate before parsing.

patterns.title: Narrow the TypeScript result
patterns.note: The bundled declaration types result.type as string rather than 'rgb' | 'hsl', so TypeScript cannot provide exhaustive model checking without your own narrower type.

patterns.title: Load the CommonJS build
patterns.note: The package's main field points to dist/index.cjs.js. Its module field provides the ESM build used by compatible bundlers.

guide.whatIs: parse-imports-exports scans a JavaScript or TypeScript source string and returns a compact inventory of its module boundary. One function identifies static imports, dynamic imports with literal paths, require calls, reexports, ESM declarations, TypeScript type-only forms, interfaces, namespaces, and CommonJS assignments. Results are grouped by syntax kind and module specifier, with source offsets and optional line-column positions. It is designed for dependency analysis and code tooling that does not need a complete syntax tree or evaluation.
useIf: You need a quick dependency inventory from already valid, consistently formatted JavaScript or TypeScript
Your tool must distinguish value imports, type-only imports, dynamic imports, require calls, reexports, and CommonJS assignments
You need source ranges for module statements but do not want the memory and traversal cost of a full AST
You ship for both ESM and CommonJS and want included TypeScript declarations from one small API
skipIf: You must accept arbitrary or half-edited source: the README explicitly says the parser works on syntactically correct, well-formatted code such as Prettier output
You need a full AST for transformations, scope analysis, comments outside module statements, or expression semantics: this API returns only categorized import and export metadata
You need module resolution: results contain raw specifiers such as ./foo or react, but the package does not apply Node exports rules, aliases, tsconfig paths, extensions, or filesystem lookup
You need a settled public contract: the current release is 0.2.4, and the result type exposes many syntax-specific optional properties whose shape can still change before 1.0

You cannot restrict source syntax to ES2018-capable runtimes: the README says the implementation uses named RegExp capture groups, and it only recognizes dynamic import targets that are string literals rather than computed expressions
guide.setupReality: Install the package and import the single parseImportsExports function. Version 0.2.4 declares ESM internally but publishes conditional import and require entry points, so both import {parseImportsExports} from 'parse-imports-exports' and const {parseImportsExports} = require('parse-imports-exports') are supported. Types are included. There is one runtime dependency, parse-statements, pinned exactly to 1.0.11. The difficult part is not installation but consuming the result correctly. The function does not return one flat dependency list. It returns separate optional maps for namedImports, namespaceImports, dynamicImports, requires, typeNamedImports, typeNamespaceImports, typeDynamicImports, six reexport groups, and several local export groups. A missing group is undefined, not an empty object. Each module path maps to a non-empty array because the same specifier can occur more than once. Aliases are keyed by the local or exported name, with by holding the original name. Source start and end offsets are always present; includeLineColumn adds strings such as 3:12 at extra processing cost. The parser records syntax problems in errors rather than promising a complete result from malformed input, so decide whether any error invalidates your analysis. Its own README requires syntactically correct, well-formatted input, making a Prettier or compiler pass a sensible upstream boundary. Options can skip CommonJS exports, dynamic imports, regular-expression literals, require calls, or string-literal shielding for speed. The last two ignore options can create false positives if source text contains import-like tokens inside skipped literals, so enable them only when the input grammar makes that safe. This tool also stops at syntax discovery: feed raw specifiers into a separate resolver if you need actual files, package export conditions, tsconfig paths, or a dependency graph.

alternatives.name: es-module-lexer
alternatives.when: You need a widely used low-level ESM lexer with exact import slices and are happy to handle a terser output format

alternatives.name: @babel/parser
alternatives.when: You need a complete JavaScript or TypeScript AST for transformations, syntax recovery, scopes, and plugin syntax

alternatives.name: acorn
alternatives.when: You want a standards-focused JavaScript parser with a full ESTree-compatible AST and a plugin ecosystem

alternatives.name: cjs-module-lexer
alternatives.when: Your main problem is fast CommonJS export and reexport detection rather than combined TypeScript and ESM reporting

guide.verdict: A useful specialized scanner when input is valid and the exact import/export categories match your tooling job. Choose a full parser when malformed code, transformations, resolution, or unfamiliar syntax must be handled correctly.

apiStability.why: There is only one runtime function, and version 0.2.4 supports both import and require with bundled types, which keeps the entry point simple. The returned contract is much larger: it has more than twenty optional syntax-specific properties, path-keyed arrays, branded names and positions, plus an errors map. Because the project remains below 1.0, consumers should isolate that shape behind their own adapter instead of spreading direct property access throughout a codebase.

docsQuality.why: The README gives an unusually comprehensive input sample and shows the corresponding result for static, dynamic, CommonJS, reexport, TypeScript type, interface, namespace, and declaration forms. It also documents every performance option and states the well-formatted-source limitation up front. Documentation is still one long page with no separate explanation of error recovery, end-offset semantics, resolver boundaries, or a compatibility matrix for newer proposal syntax.

maintenance.why: Version 0.2.4 and the repository's latest push both date to February 16, 2025. The repository is not archived and GitHub reports 2 open issues and pull requests, but there has been no visible repository push for roughly eighteen months as of this guide. The exact parse-statements 1.0.11 dependency reduces surprise from upstream drift, while also making future parser fixes dependent on a new release here.

ecosystem.why: The package recorded 4,968,139 downloads for the fetched week, publishes ESM and CommonJS builds, includes TypeScript declarations, and understands both modern ESM and several TypeScript and CommonJS forms. Its direct community footprint is small at 8 GitHub stars, and it deliberately does not provide AST tooling, path resolution, transforms, or editor integration. High installation volume therefore looks more transitive than community-led.

patterns.title: Parse imports and exports
patterns.snippet:
import {parseImportsExports} from 'parse-imports-exports'

const result = parseImportsExports(`
  import {readFile as read} from 'node:fs/promises'
  export const load = (path) => read(path, 'utf8')
`)

console.log(result.namedImports, result.declarationExports)
patterns.note: Every result group is optional and absent groups are undefined. Treat result.errors as a failed or partial analysis according to your tool's policy.

patterns.title: List static import specifiers
patterns.snippet:
const parsed = parseImportsExports(source)
const staticPaths = new Set([
  ...Object.keys(parsed.namedImports ?? {}),
  ...Object.keys(parsed.namespaceImports ?? {}),
  ...Object.keys(parsed.typeNamedImports ?? {}),
  ...Object.keys(parsed.typeNamespaceImports ?? {})
])

console.log([...staticPaths])
patterns.note: This includes type-only dependencies. Side-effect imports are represented in namedImports with position data but no default or names fields.

patterns.title: Read named imports and aliases
patterns.note: The names object is keyed by the local binding. An alias stores its original imported name in by.

patterns.title: Inspect default and namespace imports
patterns.note: Imports containing * as are placed in namespaceImports. A plain default import without a namespace is placed in namedImports.

patterns.title: Find dynamic imports and require calls
patterns.note: The scanner records literal module paths. Computed expressions such as import(prefix + name) cannot become a concrete path entry.

patterns.title: Collect all reexport sources
patterns.note: Reexports are separate from imports because they affect a package's public surface even when no local binding is created.

patterns.title: List exported runtime declarations
patterns.note: kind distinguishes const, class, async function, generators, enums, destructuring, declare forms, and other supported declaration shapes.

patterns.title: Separate TypeScript type exports
patterns.note: These groups describe declarations only. The package does not parse members or resolve relationships between the declared types.

patterns.title: Detect CommonJS assignments
patterns.snippet:
const parsed = parseImportsExports(`
  module.exports = createApp()
  module.exports.version = '1.0.0'
`)

console.log(parsed.commonJsNamespaceExport)
console.log(parsed.commonJsExports?.version)
patterns.note: module.exports = value and property assignments use separate fields. This is syntax detection, not Node runtime evaluation.

patterns.title: Add line and column positions
patterns.note: Line-column strings are optional and requested explicitly. Numeric start and end offsets remain available on every recognized statement.

patterns.title: Recover the original statement text
patterns.note: Keep the original source beside the result. Positions are metadata; the parser does not copy full statement text into each entry.

patterns.title: Skip syntax categories you do not need
patterns.note: These flags can reduce work and intentionally remove result groups. Be cautious with ignoreStringLiterals or ignoreRegexpLiterals because import-like text inside skipped literals may be misread.

guide.whatIs: parse-latin is a tokenizer for Latin-script prose. Pass a string to new ParseLatin().parse() and you get back an nlcst syntax tree: a root holding paragraphs, paragraphs holding sentences, sentences holding word, whitespace, punctuation and symbol nodes, each one carrying exact line, column and character offset. It handles the cases naive splitting gets wrong, so a period in e.g. or in a numbered list item does not end a sentence, and non-profit, she's, G.I. and 11:00 each stay a single word. It is the engine inside retext-latin, retext's default parser, which is why a repository with 57 stars sees close to four million downloads a week.
useIf: You need sentence and word boundaries with exact character offsets, for highlighters, readability scores or prose linters that point back into the source
You write or run retext plugins and want the same nlcst tree the rest of the unified ecosystem speaks
Your text mixes Latin-script languages, since the README demonstrates French, Icelandic and Old English through one tokenizer
You want a small typed dependency: 10.2 KB gzipped, six runtime dependencies all from the same family, and TypeScript types included
skipIf: You wanted linguistics: there is no part-of-speech tagging, lemmatisation, entity extraction or sentiment here, only tokenisation into a tree
Your text is specifically English or Dutch, where parse-english and parse-dutch extend this parser with language-specific abbreviation and elision rules and give better sentence breaks
You only need quick sentence or word splitting with no offsets and no tree, since Intl.Segmenter is built into Node and every current browser at zero cost
Your text is CJK, Arabic, Hebrew or another non-Latin script; the name is the scope, and the README says Cyrillic and Georgian work only somewhat

You need visible progress: no release since 7.0.0 in July 2023, no push since October 2024, and the generated character tables are built against @unicode/unicode-15.0.0, so anything added to Unicode since is unclassified
guide.setupReality: The install is trivial and the friction is around it. The package is ESM only, so require() throws in CommonJS and you need dynamic import or a bundler. The learning curve is the tree: nlcst is a unist-flavoured AST, and doing anything with it means pulling in companions such as nlcst-to-string (already one of its six dependencies), unist-util-visit and unist-util-inspect, each a separate small package. Nothing on the parser is configurable either; new ParseLatin().parse(text) is the entire documented API unless you reach into the tokenize plugin arrays. The stated support floor is Node 16, written in 2023 as 'maintained versions of Node', and that has drifted since Node 16 reached end of life in September 2023 with no new major released after it.

alternatives.name: parse-english
alternatives.when: Your text is English: the same tree plus English abbreviation and elision handling for cleaner sentence breaks

alternatives.name: compromise
alternatives.when: You want part-of-speech tagging, matching and transformation of English text rather than tokens

alternatives.name: wink-nlp
alternatives.when: You need fast tokenisation together with part-of-speech tags, entities and sentiment in one typed package

guide.verdict: Finished software in the good sense: a tiny stable API, an empty issue tracker, and it still quietly tokenises text for the whole retext ecosystem at roughly 3.8M downloads a week. Take it (or parse-english) when you need offset-accurate tokens or already live in unified, and look elsewhere for language understanding.

apiStability.why: One class exposing parse plus four tokenize methods, unchanged since 7.0.0 in July 2023; earlier majors mostly tracked Node support and the nlcst type packages rather than changing what the parser does

docsQuality.why: The README covers the whole API, spells out the tokenisation rules and the sentence exceptions, and links a live tree demo; everything about working with the resulting tree lives in the separate nlcst and unist documentation

maintenance.why: No release since July 2023 and no push since October 2024, but the tracker holds zero open issues and pull requests, so nothing is being ignored; the caveat is that the generated character tables are pinned to Unicode 15.0.0

ecosystem.why: It is the parser behind retext-latin, retext's default, which is where roughly 3.8M weekly downloads come from, and every unist utility works on its output; outside unified almost nothing consumes nlcst

patterns.title: Turn a string into an nlcst tree
patterns.note: ESM only, so require('parse-latin') throws ERR_REQUIRE_ESM and CommonJS needs await import(); whitespace containing a line break starts a new paragraph.

patterns.title: Print the tree while you are learning it
patterns.snippet:
import {ParseLatin} from 'parse-latin'
import {inspect} from 'unist-util-inspect'

console.log(inspect(new ParseLatin().parse('Hi there. Bye.')))
patterns.note: unist-util-inspect renders nested nodes with their positions, which is far more readable than console.log on a deep tree; the demo at wooorm.com/parse-latin does the same in a browser.

patterns.title: Get a flat token list
patterns.note: tokenize is the raw first pass with four categories and no sentence logic, so intra-word merging has not run and she's is still three tokens; parse or tokenizeSentence give you one word node.

patterns.title: Parse a fragment at one level
patterns.note: tokenizeSentence never splits, so the whole input becomes one sentence node with word merging applied; splitting on terminal marks and un-splitting abbreviations happens a level up in tokenizeParagraph.

patterns.title: Collect the sentences of a document
patterns.snippet:
import {ParseLatin} from 'parse-latin'
import {toString} from 'nlcst-to-string'
import {visit} from 'unist-util-visit'

const sentences = []
visit(new ParseLatin().parse(text), 'SentenceNode', (node) => {
  sentences.push(toString(node))
})
patterns.note: The reason to use this rather than splitting on periods is the exception handling: e.g., numbered items, initialisms such as G.I., and terminal marks inside closing quotes are all accounted for.

patterns.title: Count words the way the tokenizer sees them
patterns.note: A word is a run of Unicode letters or digits plus merged inner marks, so 11:00, N/A and non-profit each count once and the total will not match splitting on whitespace.

patterns.title: Read the text back out of a node
patterns.snippet:
import {toString} from 'nlcst-to-string'

const firstSentence = tree.children[0].children[0]
toString(firstSentence) // 'One sentence.'
patterns.note: Parent nodes have children rather than a value, so there is no text property to read; nlcst-to-string joins the leaves and is already one of the six dependencies.

patterns.title: Map a node back to the source string
patterns.note: Offsets round-trip against the exact input you parsed, which is what makes nlcst usable for linters; trimming or normalising the text afterwards breaks the correspondence.

patterns.title: Reach it through retext with plugins
patterns.snippet:
import {retext} from 'retext'
import retextRepeatedWords from 'retext-repeated-words'

const file = await retext()
  .use(retextRepeatedWords)
  .process('It it happens.')
console.error(String(file.messages))
patterns.note: retext's default parser is retext-latin, which is this package underneath, so let retext own the parsing rather than instantiating ParseLatin alongside it.

patterns.title: Write your own plugin over the tree
patterns.note: A plugin is a function returning a transformer that receives the tree; file.message reads the node's position on its own, so the warning lands on the right line and column.

patterns.title: Add your own pass to the tokenizer
patterns.note: The constructor copies the plugin arrays onto the instance, so mutating them leaves other parsers untouched; layering passes this way is exactly how parse-english adds its English rules.

patterns.title: Remember the character tables are frozen
patterns.snippet:
// lib/expressions.js is generated by script/build-expressions.js
// against @unicode/unicode-15.0.0 code point tables
patterns.note: Characters and scripts added to Unicode after 15.0.0 fall outside the generated letter, mark and punctuation classes, so newly assigned code points may tokenize as symbols rather than as parts of words.

guide.whatIs: parse-statements is a dependency-free source-text scanner that finds ordered sequences of regular-expression tokens and reports the token offsets through callbacks. You describe statement shapes and optional comment delimiters, create a parser once, then let it mutate a context object as it walks a string. It can recognize lightweight constructs across different languages, but it is not a grammar parser: it does not build an AST, understand nesting, or validate a language beyond the token sequences you supply.
useIf: You need to extract a few predictable statement shapes from source text without installing a full language parser
Your format has comments between meaningful tokens and you need their exact source offsets
You want one configured scanner reused against many strings while accumulating results in a caller-owned context
You need both ESM and CommonJS entry points plus bundled TypeScript declarations
skipIf: You need a correct JavaScript, TypeScript, SQL, or CSS syntax tree: this package matches regular-expression token sequences and does not model grammar or nesting
Statements can overlap or a later match should supersede an earlier one; the README explicitly says statements cannot overlap and matching advances through the source
You need best-match or backtracking behavior: each statement is an ordered token chain, so an early plausible token can lead to the incomplete-statement callback instead of a smarter parse
Your runtime lacks ES2018 named capture groups or is Node.js older than 10, both listed as compatibility requirements
You want a large user-facing ecosystem or extensive troubleshooting material: the repository has 12 stars, and documentation is one dense README centered on a single long example
guide.setupReality: There are no runtime dependencies, native builds, credentials, or config files. Install the package, import createParseFunction, and define a mutable context plus statement descriptors. Most of the setup cost is escaping and parser design. Every token is a string passed to RegExp, not a RegExp object, and the default flags are gmu; a backslash must therefore survive both JavaScript string parsing and RegExp construction, so word boundaries look like '\b' in source. The scanner only knows comments you describe with opening and closing token pairs. Set canIncludeComments on each statement that permits them, and use shouldSearchBeforeComments when a statement opener and comment opener can start at the same position. Callbacks receive numeric start and end offsets, with end exclusive, so use source.slice(start, end). An incomplete statement calls its local onError with only the tokens found so far. An unclosed comment calls the comment error handler and stops parsing. A statement callback may return a replacement end index, but if it moves past comments you must parse those comments yourself, as the README warns. Custom regexpFlags replace the defaults rather than extending them, so omitting g can break the global scanning design. TypeScript can type a fixed token count through OnParse<Context, N>, but heterogeneous descriptors often require a broader OnParse cast, as the official example demonstrates.

alternatives.name: esprima
alternatives.when: Use it when the input is JavaScript and you need a standards-aware ESTree syntax tree

alternatives.name: @babel/parser
alternatives.when: Use it for JavaScript or TypeScript syntax, proposals, JSX, and parser error recovery

alternatives.name: meriyah
alternatives.when: Use it for a fast ECMAScript parser when a real AST matters more than a tiny generic scanner

guide.verdict: A focused tool for token-sequence extraction when a full parser would be excessive. Do not mistake its language-neutral input for language understanding; nested or ambiguous syntax deserves a real grammar parser.

apiStability.why: The package remains on major version 1 and exposes one runtime function, createParseFunction, with callback-driven descriptors and exported TypeScript types. That small public surface limits breakage risk. The tradeoff is that subtle behavior lives in callback ordering, index overrides, regular-expression flags, and comment precedence, so changing a token definition can alter parsing even when the package API itself stays fixed.

docsQuality.why: The README documents every option, callback signature, token offset, comment pair, default regexp flag, runtime requirement, and the special callback return value. It also includes a substantial import/export example. However, the material is dense, there is no separate reference site, and common recipes such as quoted strings, nested delimiters, or testing malformed input are not broken into approachable examples.

maintenance.why: Version 1.0.12 was published May 6, 2025 and the repository was pushed minutes before that release. It is not archived and GitHub reports no open issues or pull requests. This is credible maintenance evidence for a small, finished utility, although there has been no repository push for more than a year and the tiny contributor footprint leaves continuity dependent on a narrow maintainer base.

ecosystem.why: npm records 4,962,664 downloads in the latest week, but the repository has only 12 stars, suggesting much of its reach may arrive transitively rather than through a broad direct-user community. It has no runtime dependencies, provides ESM and CommonJS exports, and bundles types. There are no documented plugins, grammar packs, editor integrations, or language-specific extensions around it.

patterns.title: Extract a simple begin-to-end statement
patterns.note: Token strings are passed to RegExp, so backslashes such as the one in \b must be escaped in JavaScript source.

patterns.title: Slice the complete matched statement
patterns.note: start is inclusive and end is exclusive, which matches String.prototype.slice without adjustment.

patterns.title: Record an incomplete token sequence
patterns.note: onError receives only the statement tokens found before the sequence became incomplete.

patterns.title: Collect line comments
patterns.note: The closing token is a regular expression too; the README uses $\n? to end a line comment.

patterns.title: Collect block comments and reject unclosed ones
patterns.note: An unclosed comment ends the parse after the comment error callback runs.

patterns.title: Allow comments between statement tokens
patterns.note: Comments are attached to the preceding parsed token; shouldSearchBeforeComments controls precedence when openers compete.

patterns.title: Read comments attached between tokens
patterns.note: Only non-final tokens can have a comments property because comments are stored between a token and its successor.

patterns.title: Surface parser-internal mismatches
patterns.note: This global callback is distinct from a statement's incomplete-sequence callback and a comment's missing-close callback.

patterns.title: Continue scanning from a custom index
patterns.note: If the custom range crosses comments, the callback must account for them because the scanner resumes only at the returned index.

patterns.title: Reuse one parser with separate contexts
patterns.note: The parser mutates the context passed to each call and does not create or return a result object for you.

guide.whatIs: partial-json parses JSON strings that are cut off mid-stream. When an LLM streams a JSON response token by token, JSON.parse fails on every chunk until the very last one; partial-json's parse function instead returns the best complete value it can build from what has arrived so far, so you can render structured data live while it streams. An Allow bitmask controls which types may be incomplete: with STR a half-finished string is returned as-is, without it the parser waits for the closing quote. It is a small pure-JavaScript library with zero dependencies and both CJS and ESM builds.
useIf: You stream JSON from an LLM (tool arguments, structured output) and want to update the UI on every chunk instead of waiting for the final token
You want JSON.parse-compatible behavior on complete input with graceful handling of truncated input, in one function
You need control over what may be partial, for example allow half-open objects but suppress half-finished string values so users never see cut-off text
You need to salvage a value from a response that hit a max-token limit and ended mid-object
skipIf: Your JSON is malformed rather than truncated: partial-json throws on actually invalid input like single quotes or trailing commas, which is jsonrepair territory
You use the Vercel AI SDK or another framework whose streamObject/structured-output helpers already do incremental parsing internally, in which case adding this is redundant
You process multi-megabyte streams where you need incremental event-based parsing: this library reparses the full accumulated string on every call, which is O(n) per chunk and O(n^2) over a stream
You want a battle-hardened core dependency: this is a 0.x package from a small maintainer with sparse commit activity, fine as a UI nicety, riskier as a load-bearing parser
guide.setupReality: npm i partial-json and you are done: zero dependencies, TypeScript types included, works in Node and browsers with both require and import. The things to internalize are behavioral, not install-related. parse defaults to Allow.ALL, which will happily return half-written strings and numbers, so decide your bitmask deliberately. You also still own the streaming loop: accumulate chunks into one string yourself and call parse on each update, and wrap calls in try/catch because a chunk boundary can still leave text the parser considers malformed rather than merely incomplete.

alternatives.name: jsonrepair
alternatives.when: Your input is broken JSON (quotes, commas, comments), not just truncated JSON, and you want it fixed into valid output.

alternatives.name: best-effort-json-parser
alternatives.when: You want maximally forgiving parsing of messy partial JSON without configuring what may be incomplete.

alternatives.name: @streamparser/json
alternatives.when: You need true incremental SAX-style parsing of large JSON streams without reparsing from the start.

guide.verdict: The standard small tool for one specific job: showing structured LLM output while it streams, which explains 5M+ weekly downloads on 243 stars. Use it for that; for repairing invalid JSON or parsing huge streams pick a different tool.

apiStability.why: Still 0.x, but the surface is two exports (parse and Allow) that have not changed in years; there is very little API to break.

docsQuality.why: The README covers the whole API with clear examples and there is a live demo, but that is all the documentation there is; edge-case behavior you learn by experiment.

maintenance.why: Last push June 2026 and only 5 open issues, but it is a small single-org project with an infrequent release cadence; low activity is partly low surface area.

ecosystem.why: Massive incidental reach because AI SDKs and LLM apps pull it in, with a matching Python implementation, but there are no plugins or tooling around it and few third-party resources.

patterns.title: Parse complete JSON like JSON.parse
patterns.note: On complete input parse behaves like JSON.parse, so you can use one code path for both mid-stream and final payloads.

patterns.title: Parse a truncated string with defaults
patterns.note: The default allowance is Allow.ALL, so everything including half-finished strings is returned; pass a bitmask if that is too eager.

patterns.title: Choose which types may be incomplete
patterns.note: Types not in the mask only appear once the parser is sure they are complete; note the unclosed object itself needs OBJ in the mask.

patterns.title: Render streamed LLM JSON incrementally
patterns.note: You accumulate the full string and reparse each time; that is fine for typical LLM response sizes but is quadratic over very long streams.

patterns.title: Suppress half-finished string values in a UI
patterns.note: Useful when showing a cut-off URL or sentence would confuse users; keys and completed values still stream in as they finish.

patterns.title: Import allowance flags without the Allow object
patterns.snippet:
import { parse, STR, OBJ, ARR } from "partial-json";

const result = parse(buffer, STR | OBJ | ARR);
patterns.note: Each Allow property is also a named export; the values are plain numbers combined with bitwise OR.

patterns.title: Handle NaN and Infinity literals
patterns.note: These are not valid JSON, but Python's json.dumps emits them, so the parser accepts them; gate with Allow.SPECIAL if you do not want partial forms.

patterns.title: Distinguish truncated from malformed input
patterns.note: Truncated JSON returns a value; genuinely invalid JSON throws MalformedJSON. Do not use this library expecting repair of bad syntax.

patterns.title: Allow partial literals like tru and nul
patterns.note: With the matching atom flag the parser commits to the only literal the prefix can become; without it the element is omitted until complete.

patterns.title: Use the convenience flag groups
patterns.note: Allow.COLLECTION is the common choice for UIs: structure streams in live while every scalar value waits until it is complete.

guide.whatIs: passlib is a password hashing framework rather than a single hash function. It wraps over thirty schemes behind one interface, from modern ones such as argon2, bcrypt and pbkdf2_sha256 down to whatever is sitting in an old /etc/shadow file or a 2007 phpBB database, and each handler exposes the same hash(), verify() and identify() calls. The piece people actually come for is CryptContext: you declare a list of schemes in preference order, mark the old ones deprecated, and then verify_and_update() checks a password against whichever scheme the stored hash uses and hands you back a freshly rehashed value when the old one is out of date. That is how you migrate a user table off md5 without asking anyone to reset their password. It also ships passlib.totp for time-based one-time passwords with encrypted secret storage. It is capable software and it is also frozen: 1.7.4 was published on 2020-10-08 and nothing has been released since.
useIf: You inherited stored hashes in a format nobody wants to touch: /etc/shadow entries, old Django or Drupal or phpBB tables, MySQL's OLD_PASSWORD, LDAP RFC-2307 strings. passlib reads them all and is the shortest path to verifying a login against them

You need to migrate hashes in place. CryptContext with deprecated='auto' plus verify_and_update() gives you the whole upgrade story in one call: correct password, old scheme detected, new hash returned for you to store
You need to identify a hash you were handed. context.identify(hash) tells you which scheme produced it, which is the first thing you want during a security audit or a database import

You want TOTP with the storage problem solved. passlib.totp with TOTP.using(secrets={...}) encrypts the shared secret at rest with an application key and handles key rotation, which is more than most standalone TOTP libraries offer
skipIf: You are starting a new project. There is one correct answer for a new password column in 2026 (argon2id, or bcrypt if your infrastructure demands it) and you can get it from argon2-cffi or pwdlib in ten lines without a framework that also knows how to read lmhash

You use bcrypt and cannot pin its version. passlib 1.7.4's bcrypt backend probes for an ancient wraparound bug at load time by hashing a test password longer than 72 bytes. bcrypt 5.0 raises ValueError on anything over 72 bytes instead of truncating, so the probe throws and every single bcrypt.hash() call fails with 'password cannot be longer than 72 bytes'. Verified on bcrypt 5.0.0. Your only fix is pinning bcrypt<5, which means freezing a security-critical native library because an unmaintained wrapper cannot be patched

You object to warnings you cannot silence. On any bcrypt from 4.1 onward passlib logs '(trapped) error reading bcrypt version' with an AttributeError traceback, because it reads bcrypt.__about__.__version__ and that attribute is gone. Harmless, permanent, and it appears in production logs on every process start

The defaults matter to you. pbkdf2_sha256.default_rounds is 29000 in 1.7.4, set years before current guidance and never revised because there have been no releases. Anyone who calls pbkdf2_sha256.hash(pw) without an explicit rounds value gets a work factor that would not pass a review today

You are on Python 3.13 or newer and rely on OS crypt. PEP 594 removed the stdlib crypt module; passlib guards the import so it still runs, but passlib.utils.has_crypt flips to False and sha256_crypt and sha512_crypt quietly fall back to passlib's pure-Python implementations. Same output, different code path, noticeably slower, and nothing tells you the switch happened

You need a maintained dependency in your security stack. The last release is 1.7.4 from 2020-10-08. The Heptapod tracker shows activity as recently as April 2026 but no release has followed, the code still carries Python 2 compatibility shims, and there is no GitHub repo to file against. Auditors ask about this
You only need one scheme. Pulling in thirty of them, including des_crypt, lmhash, nthash and mysql323, expands the code your security review has to reason about for no benefit
guide.setupReality: pip install passlib is instant and pure Python, but the useful configurations need extras and each has a catch. passlib[bcrypt] installs the bcrypt package, and you must pin it below 5.0 or the backend is dead on arrival with a ValueError from passlib's own compatibility probe; even bcrypt 4.x logs an AttributeError traceback about a missing __about__ attribute on every process start. passlib[argon2] pulls argon2-cffi, which needs a wheel or a C toolchain, and this is the combination that still works cleanly on Python 3.13. passlib[totp] needs cryptography for secret encryption. There is no requires_python declared on the wheel, so pip will happily install it on runtimes it was never tested against. Nothing warns you that on Python 3.13 the stdlib crypt module is gone and the OS-backed schemes have silently switched to pure-Python fallbacks. If you use bcrypt, remember that the algorithm itself truncates at 72 bytes and modern bcrypt raises rather than truncating, so long passphrases and multi-byte characters need a pre-hash step you write yourself. Pin every one of these versions in your lockfile, because the failure modes arrive through your transitive dependencies rather than through passlib.

alternatives.name: pwdlib
alternatives.when: You want a small maintained replacement with the same hash/verify/needs-update shape and only modern schemes

alternatives.name: argon2-cffi
alternatives.when: You need argon2id and nothing else, with sensible current defaults and active maintenance

alternatives.name: bcrypt
alternatives.when: Policy or an existing hash column requires bcrypt and you would rather call it directly than through a wrapper that breaks on version 5

alternatives.name: cryptography
alternatives.when: You need PBKDF2, Scrypt or key derivation as part of a wider cryptographic stack rather than password storage alone

guide.verdict: Still the best tool in Python for reading and migrating legacy password hashes, and verify_and_update() alone can justify keeping it in an old codebase. Do not reach for it in anything new: a library whose last release predates both bcrypt 5 and the removal of the crypt module is not where your password storage should live.

apiStability.why: Perfectly stable, for the reason you would rather it were not. The CryptContext and handler APIs have not changed since 1.7.0 in 2016 and cannot change, because nothing has been released since 1.7.4 on 2020-10-08. Code written a decade ago runs unmodified.

docsQuality.why: passlib.readthedocs.io is unusually thorough for a library this size: a narrative introduction, a page per handler documenting the format string and every keyword, a whole chapter on hash migration, and honest discussion of relative scheme strength. What it cannot cover is everything that broke after 2020, so the bcrypt 5 failure, the __about__ warning and the Python 3.13 crypt removal are absent and you find them in your own traceback.

maintenance.why: Effectively abandoned as a shipping product. The last release is 1.7.4 from 2020-10-08, almost six years ago. The Heptapod project shows a last activity timestamp of 2026-04-24, so someone is still reading the tracker, but the two known breakages against current bcrypt and current Python have sat unreleased. For a password hashing library that is the most serious mark on this page.

ecosystem.why: Roughly 9.3M weekly downloads and still embedded in a generation of Django, Flask and FastAPI tutorials, so it is present in an enormous number of production stacks. The direction of travel is away from it: FastAPI's own documentation moved to pwdlib, and new projects reach for argon2-cffi or bcrypt directly.

patterns.title: Hash and verify with an explicit work factor
patterns.snippet:
from passlib.hash import pbkdf2_sha256

hasher = pbkdf2_sha256.using(rounds=600_000)
stored = hasher.hash('correct horse battery staple')

print(stored[:30])   # $pbkdf2-sha256$600000$...
print(pbkdf2_sha256.verify('correct horse battery staple', stored))  # True
patterns.note: Always go through .using(rounds=...). pbkdf2_sha256.default_rounds is 29000 in 1.7.4 and has not been revised since, so the bare pbkdf2_sha256.hash(pw) you see in most tutorials produces a work factor set for hardware from another decade.

patterns.title: Declare a context with a preferred scheme and deprecated ones
patterns.snippet:
from passlib.context import CryptContext

pwd = CryptContext(
    schemes=['argon2', 'pbkdf2_sha256', 'sha512_crypt', 'des_crypt'],
    deprecated='auto',
    argon2__memory_cost=65536,
    argon2__time_cost=3,
)

hashed = pwd.hash('secret')   # uses argon2, the first scheme
patterns.note: The first scheme in the list is what new hashes use; everything after it is accepted on verify only. deprecated='auto' marks every scheme except the first as needing an upgrade, and the double-underscore keywords are how you pass per-scheme settings.

patterns.title: Upgrade a hash during a successful login
patterns.note: This is the reason passlib is still in codebases. new_hash is None when the stored hash is already current, so the branch stays cheap. The rehash uses the plaintext you already have in hand, which is the only moment you get to do it without a password reset email.

patterns.title: Work out which scheme produced a stored hash
patterns.snippet:
legacy = 'A7Tt6IjNRAIL.'
print(pwd.identify(legacy))          # 'des_crypt'
print(pwd.needs_update(legacy))      # True

from passlib.registry import list_crypt_handlers
print(len(list_crypt_handlers()))    # 77 registered names
patterns.note: identify() returns None when no configured scheme recognizes the string, which is also what a corrupted or truncated column looks like, so audit both cases. It only checks schemes in the context, not all 77 handlers passlib knows about.

patterns.title: Use argon2id with parameters you chose
patterns.snippet:
from passlib.hash import argon2

print(argon2.default_rounds, argon2.memory_cost, argon2.parallelism)
# 3 65536 4

h = argon2.using(memory_cost=131072, time_cost=4, parallelism=2).hash('secret')
print(h[:34])  # $argon2id$v=19$m=131072,t=4,p=2$
patterns.note: This needs argon2-cffi installed via passlib[argon2] and is the backend combination that still behaves correctly on Python 3.13. The parameters are encoded in the hash string, so old hashes keep verifying with their original settings after you raise the defaults.

patterns.title: Keep the bcrypt backend working at all
patterns.snippet:
# pyproject.toml / requirements.txt
#   passlib[bcrypt]==1.7.4
#   bcrypt<5

from passlib.hash import bcrypt
print(bcrypt.using(rounds=12).hash('secret')[:15])  # $2b$12$...
patterns.note: On bcrypt 5.0 this raises ValueError('password cannot be longer than 72 bytes') for any input, because passlib probes for an old wraparound bug by hashing a test string longer than 72 bytes at backend load. On bcrypt 4.x it works but logs a trapped AttributeError about bcrypt.__about__ every time the backend loads.

patterns.title: Handle passphrases longer than bcrypt's 72-byte limit
patterns.note: bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes, and multi-byte characters hit that limit far sooner than 72 visible characters. Base64 the digest rather than passing raw bytes: that keeps the input to 44 printable ASCII bytes and sidesteps the historical disagreements between bcrypt implementations over embedded null bytes. Whichever pre-hash you pick, it has to be applied identically on hash and on verify forever.

patterns.title: Avoid leaking which usernames exist
patterns.note: Without dummy_verify() an unknown username returns in microseconds while a real one takes the full hash time, and that difference is measurable over a network. It returns False and never raises, so it drops straight into the miss branch.

patterns.title: Verify a hash from /etc/shadow
patterns.snippet:
from passlib.hash import sha512_crypt
import passlib.utils

print(passlib.utils.has_crypt)   # False on Python 3.13+
print(sha512_crypt.verify('secret', shadow_entry))
patterns.note: On Python 3.12 and earlier this calls the OS crypt(3). On 3.13 the stdlib crypt module is gone, has_crypt becomes False, and passlib silently uses its own pure-Python implementation. Results match, speed does not, and no warning is emitted.

patterns.title: Load hashing policy from a config file
patterns.snippet:
pwd = CryptContext.from_string("""
[passlib]
schemes = argon2, pbkdf2_sha256, sha512_crypt
deprecated = auto
argon2__memory_cost = 65536
pbkdf2_sha256__rounds = 600000
""")

pwd.update(argon2__time_cost=4)   # bump without a redeploy of code
patterns.note: Keeping the policy in config lets you raise cost parameters without touching application code, and from_path() reads the same ini format from disk. Changing settings does not invalidate existing hashes, since each stored string carries the parameters it was created with.

patterns.title: Issue and check TOTP codes with encrypted secrets
patterns.snippet:
from passlib.totp import TOTP, generate_secret

# generate_secret() once, store it in your app config, never in the database
Factory = TOTP.using(secrets={'1': APP_TOTP_KEY})

totp = Factory(new=True)
uri = totp.to_uri(issuer='example.com', label='ada@example.com')
blob = totp.to_json()    # {"enckey": ...} encrypted at rest
patterns.note: TOTP.using(secrets=...) encrypts the shared secret with your application key before it reaches the database, and the numeric tag lets you rotate keys while old rows still decrypt. This path needs the cryptography package from passlib[totp].

patterns.title: Validate a submitted TOTP token
patterns.snippet:
from passlib.exc import TokenError

totp = Factory.from_json(user.totp_blob)
try:
    match = totp.match(submitted_token, last_counter=user.totp_last_counter)
except TokenError as exc:
    raise AuthError(str(exc))

user.totp_last_counter = match.counter   # blocks replay of the same code
patterns.note: match() raises rather than returning False: a wrong code gives InvalidTokenError and a malformed one gives MalformedTokenError, both subclasses of TokenError. Persisting match.counter is what stops an attacker replaying a code that is still inside its window.

guide.whatIs: Passport is authentication middleware for Express-style Node apps. Its whole job is to run a request through a named strategy and, on success, put the result on req.user. Everything provider-specific lives in a separate strategy package, and the site advertises over 500 of them covering passwords, OAuth providers, SAML, OpenID Connect and JWT. What it deliberately does not do is the rest of authentication: no routes, no user storage, no password hashing, no email verification, no CSRF, no rate limiting. The core is three small dependencies at 2.9 KB gzipped, and it has not changed since 0.7.0 was published in November 2023.
useIf: You maintain an Express app already running on Passport, where the behaviour is known and a decade of answers exists for every failure mode
You need an identity provider whose only usable Node integration is an existing Passport strategy, which is still true for plenty of SAML and regional OAuth providers
You want the smallest possible hook into authentication and intend to own sessions, storage and hashing yourself as a deliberate choice
You are on Nest.js, where the @nestjs/passport wrapper makes it the path of least resistance inside that framework
skipIf: You are starting something new: no commit since August 2024, the only release since 2022 is 0.7.0 from November 2023, 398 open issues and pull requests, and it is still 0.x after fifteen years

You assume the strategies are healthier than the core, because they are not: passport-local's newest npm release is 1.0.0 from March 2014, passport-jwt was last pushed February 2024 and passport-google-oauth2 May 2023
Your runtime is not Express-shaped (Next.js route handlers, Hono, Fastify idioms, edge or serverless), since the middleware model mutates req and res in ways those environments resist
You want the surrounding features: hashing, verification emails, 2FA, organisations and rate limiting are all yours to build, and current alternatives ship them
The done(err, user) callback style bothers you: it predates promises, so in an async codebase every strategy becomes try/catch glue around a callback
guide.setupReality: npm install passport gets you nothing runnable on its own. Each auth method is a separate package with its own maintainer and health record, and around it you still need express-session with a real store (the default MemoryStore leaks and forgets everything on restart), your own serializeUser and deserializeUser, and your own hashing inside the verify callback. The failures are quiet rather than loud: wrong middleware order gives redirect loops with nothing in the logs, and a missing body parser means the strategy never receives credentials at all. Version drift is the other trap, because 0.6.0 made req.logout asynchronous and made a successful login regenerate the session, which invalidated most tutorials written before May 2022, and thin official docs mean those tutorials are exactly what you will find.

alternatives.name: better-auth
alternatives.when: A new TypeScript project that wants complete authentication (passwords, OAuth, 2FA, organisations) from one actively developed framework rather than a middleware kit

alternatives.name: next-auth
alternatives.when: A Next.js app, where Auth.js fits route handlers and edge runtimes that the middleware model does not

alternatives.name: openid-client
alternatives.when: You want certified low-level OAuth 2 and OpenID Connect flows and are content owning sessions and user storage

guide.verdict: A dormant core with an enormous installed base: 7.8M weekly downloads against a repository untouched for two years and flagship strategies that are quieter still. Keeping it in a running Express app is defensible; picking it for something new is not, because the strategy breadth that justified it now exists in maintained alternatives with far less wiring.

apiStability.why: The API has barely moved in a decade and 0.7.0 changed almost nothing, which is a kind of stability; against that, it is still 0.x after fifteen years and 0.6.0 broke most published guides in one release with async req.logout and session regeneration on login

docsQuality.why: passportjs.org covers happy paths thinly and says little about the session mechanics (regeneration, serialisation, middleware order) behind most real bugs; per-strategy documentation ranges from adequate to absent, so learning happens through third-party tutorials of mixed vintage, many of them predating 0.6.0

maintenance.why: No push since 2024-08-16, no release since November 2023, 398 open issues and pull requests, and a largely solo author spread across hundreds of strategy packages; that is dormancy rather than a finished project being tended

ecosystem.why: The advertised 500-plus strategies and 7.8M weekly downloads are real, but the flagships are frozen: passport-local last published in 2014, passport-jwt last pushed February 2024, passport-google-oauth2 May 2023, so the usable ecosystem is smaller and older than the count suggests

patterns.title: Wire it into Express in the order that works
patterns.note: Body parsing and express-session both have to be registered before passport.session(); getting it wrong produces redirect loops or empty credentials with no error anywhere.

patterns.title: Verify a username and password
patterns.note: done(null, false) means the credentials were wrong; done(err) means your code broke. Conflating them turns a bad password into a 500.

patterns.title: Decide what goes in the session
patterns.note: deserializeUser runs on every request carrying a session, so an uncached lookup here is one database query per page view across the entire app.

patterns.title: Authenticate a login POST
patterns.note: When every attempt lands on the failure redirect with a silent log, suspect the body parser first: the strategy never saw any credentials.

patterns.title: Keep pre-login session data through login
patterns.note: Since 0.6.0 a successful login regenerates the session id and drops what was in it, so carts and return-to URLs vanish; enable this only where you store pre-login state, since it softens the session fixation defence.

patterns.title: Log the user out
patterns.note: The callback has been mandatory since 0.6.0; the synchronous req.logout() in older tutorials throws at runtime.

patterns.title: Guard a route behind login
patterns.note: No guard middleware ships with the package, so everyone writes this by hand or adds connect-ensure-login, which is itself long unmaintained.

patterns.title: Handle the result yourself for a JSON API
patterns.note: With a custom callback the session is no longer established for you; omitting req.logIn is the classic bug where login succeeds and the next request is anonymous.

patterns.title: Stateless token auth
patterns.note: session: false matters on token APIs or a cookie session gets established that nothing will ever read; passport-jwt itself has not been pushed since February 2024, so audit it like any dormant dependency.

patterns.title: Sign in with Google
patterns.note: callbackURL has to match the Google console entry exactly including protocol and port, and a mismatch surfaces on Google's consent screen rather than in your logs; use an absolute URL behind a proxy.

patterns.title: Tell the user why login failed
patterns.note: failureMessage appends to req.session.messages and never clears it, so empty the array after rendering or old errors accumulate; the older failureFlash option needs the abandoned connect-flash package.

patterns.title: Accept more than one auth method
patterns.note: Strategies run in array order and the first success wins, but the response status when all of them fail comes from the last failure, not the first.

guide.whatIs: pathspec answers one question well: does this file path match this set of gitignore-style patterns? You compile pattern lines (usually straight out of a .gitignore) into a PathSpec object, then test single paths, filter iterables of paths, or walk a directory tree. It ships two implementations: PathSpec with the 'gitignore' pattern type follows the gitignore documentation literally, while GitIgnoreSpec replicates what Git actually does, including the undocumented edge cases like negations re-including files from excluded directories. It is pure Python with zero required dependencies, and its enormous download count comes from being the ignore engine inside tools like Black and MkDocs.
useIf: Your tool needs to respect .gitignore files the way Git does: GitIgnoreSpec exists precisely for that and matches Git's edge cases, not just the docs
You let users configure include/exclude rules and want them to write familiar gitignore syntax instead of raw regex or fnmatch globs
You need to filter thousands of paths and can install an optional speedup: the backend parameter switches matching to google-re2 or hyperscan for large pattern sets
You want zero required dependencies in a library of your own, since pathspec adds nothing else to your dependency tree
skipIf: You just need simple glob matching on a few paths: fnmatch and pathlib.PurePath.match are in the standard library and cost nothing

You migrated from 0.x without reading the upgrade guide: 1.0 (January 2026) renamed 'gitwildmatch' to 'gitignore' and changed matching behavior for patterns like foo/*, so pinned-then-bumped projects can silently match different files
You need general-purpose advanced globbing (brace expansion, extglob, globstar controls) rather than gitignore semantics: wcmatch covers that ground better
This is a one-person project with a small bus factor; it is steadily maintained but there is no team behind it, which matters if you build a core product feature on its exact matching behavior
guide.setupReality: pip install pathspec is as easy as installs get: pure Python, no compiled parts, Python 3.9+. The gotchas are semantic. You must pick between PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ...) and GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(...), and the two disagree on real-world patterns; if the goal is 'behave like Git', use GitIgnoreSpec, full stop. Paths are matched as relative strings, so passing absolute paths against patterns written for a repo root quietly matches nothing. Directory patterns need the trailing slash exactly as in gitignore. And if you came from 0.x, 'gitwildmatch' still works but is deprecated with different edge-case behavior than the new 'gitignore' type, which is an easy source of confusing diffs.

alternatives.name: gitignore-parser
alternatives.when: You want a tiny single-purpose parser for one .gitignore file and do not need tree walking or combined specs.

alternatives.name: wcmatch
alternatives.when: You need advanced general globbing (extglob, brace expansion, globstar) beyond gitignore semantics.

guide.verdict: The standard way to do gitignore matching in Python, proven inside Black and MkDocs; use GitIgnoreSpec when fidelity to Git matters. Skip it when stdlib fnmatch would do, and read the 1.0 upgrade notes before bumping from 0.x.

apiStability.why: The core from_lines/match_file surface has been steady for years, but the 1.0 release in January 2026 renamed the main pattern type, deprecated GitWildMatchPattern, and changed matching edge cases, so the 0.x to 1.x jump needs care.

docsQuality.why: The README tutorial and Read the Docs reference cover the API, and the upgrade guide is honest about behavior changes, but explanations of the PathSpec vs GitIgnoreSpec split stay terse and examples are thin.

maintenance.why: Steady releases through 2026 (1.0 in January, 1.1.1 in April), pushed June 2026, and only 8 open issues and PRs; the limiting factor is that it is a single-maintainer project.

ecosystem.why: Around 173M weekly downloads because major tools like Black and MkDocs depend on it, so it is battle-tested everywhere, though there is little plugin ecosystem around such a focused library.

patterns.title: Compile gitignore-style patterns
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', [
    '*.pyc',
    'build/',
    '!build/keep.txt',
])
print(spec.match_file('module.pyc'))  # True
patterns.note: Since 1.0 the pattern type is named 'gitignore'; the old 'gitwildmatch' name still works but is deprecated and keeps slightly different edge-case behavior.

patterns.title: Load patterns from a .gitignore file
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

with open('.gitignore') as fh:
    spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(fh)

print(spec.match_file('dist/app.tar.gz'))
patterns.note: from_lines accepts any iterable of lines, so the open file object can be passed directly; comments and blank lines are handled like Git does.

patterns.title: Match exactly like Git, edge cases included
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines([
    'logs/',
    '!logs/important.log',
])
print(spec.match_file('logs/debug.log'))      # True
print(spec.match_file('logs/important.log'))  # False (re-included)
patterns.note: GitIgnoreSpec replicates Git's real behavior, including negations inside excluded directories, where plain PathSpec follows the documentation instead.

patterns.title: Check one path
patterns.snippet:
from pathlib import PurePath
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['docs/**/*.md'])
spec.match_file('docs/guide/intro.md')      # True
spec.match_file(PurePath('docs/README.md')) # pathlib works too
patterns.note: Paths are matched as given, relative to the implied root of the patterns; absolute paths against repo-relative patterns will not match.

patterns.title: Filter an existing list of paths
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['*.tmp', 'cache/'])
files = ['a.txt', 'b.tmp', 'cache/x.json']
ignored = set(spec.match_files(files))
kept = [f for f in files if f not in ignored]
patterns.note: match_files returns a generator of the matching (ignored) entries; wrap it in set or list before reusing it.

patterns.title: Walk a directory tree for matches
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['**/*.log'])
for rel_path in spec.match_tree_files('/var/app'):
    print(rel_path)
patterns.note: Yields paths relative to the root you pass in, walking the filesystem for you; use match_files instead if you already have the path list.

patterns.title: Invert matching to select files to keep
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(open('.gitignore'))
keep = set(spec.match_tree_files('project/', negate=True))
patterns.note: Specs positively match the ignored files by default; negate=True flips the result, which is what backup and packaging tools usually want.

patterns.title: Combine multiple pattern sources
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

base = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', open('.gitignore'))
local = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', open('.gitignore.local'))
spec = base + local  # later patterns win, like nested .gitignore files
patterns.note: The + operator concatenates pattern lists, preserving order, so later negations can re-include files excluded by earlier specs.

patterns.title: Speed up matching with an alternate regex backend
patterns.snippet:
# pip install 'pathspec[re2]'
from pathspec import GitIgnoreSpec

spec = GitIgnoreSpec.from_lines(lines, backend='re2')
# or backend='hyperscan', or the default backend='best'
patterns.note: New in 1.0. The default 'best' picks the fastest installed backend; re2 tends to win at high pattern counts per the project's own benchmarks.

patterns.title: Find out which pattern matched
patterns.snippet:
from pathspec import PathSpec

spec = PathSpec.from_lines('gitignore', ['*.log', '!keep.log'])
result = spec.check_file('debug.log')
print(result.include)  # True if ignored
print(result.index)    # index of the deciding pattern
patterns.note: check_file returns a result object instead of a bare bool, which is what you need for 'why is this file ignored' debugging output.

guide.whatIs: patsy turns R-style model formulas into numeric design matrices. You hand it a string like "y ~ x + C(group) + np.log(size)" plus a DataFrame, and it returns numpy arrays or DataFrames with the intercept column added, categorical variables dummy-coded against a reference level, interactions expanded, and every column given a readable name. The important trick is that it remembers what it did: the DesignInfo object attached to the result stores the category levels it saw, the mean it centered by, and the spline knots it picked, so you can rebuild the exact same columns for new rows at prediction time. It is the formula engine underneath statsmodels, which is why most people install it without ever importing it directly.
useIf: You already use statsmodels formula API (smf.ols("y ~ x + C(g)", data=df)); statsmodels 0.14 imports patsy across dozens of its modules, so it is already in your environment and worth understanding

You need training-time and prediction-time encoding to match exactly: build_design_matrices(design_info, new_df) replays the same category levels, reference cells, centering means, and spline knots instead of re-fitting them on the new rows

You are porting model code from R and want the same formula semantics: y ~ x*g for main effects plus interaction, y ~ x - 1 to drop the intercept, C(g, Treatment(reference='b')) to set the baseline, I(x + 1) to escape arithmetic
You want dummy columns with names you can read in a coefficient table (g[T.b], x:g[T.c]) rather than the positional output of pandas.get_dummies stitched together by hand
skipIf: You are starting something new. The README says it plainly: patsy is no longer under active development, no new features are planned, and the maintainers recommend migrating to Formulaic. The 2026 commits are dependabot bumps and pre-commit updates, not fixes
You want speed or sparse output. patsy materializes dense numpy arrays and only understands numpy and pandas; Formulaic is the successor written for performance and covers more dataframe backends

Your model lives in scikit-learn. ColumnTransformer plus OneHotEncoder is the idiomatic path there, it survives cross-validation and pickling, and patsy's DesignInfo does not plug into the sklearn estimator API

You would build formula strings from user input. patsy evaluates factor expressions as Python in the caller's stack frame, so "__import__('os').system('...')" in a formula is a shell, not a syntax error
You only need one-hot encoding of two columns. Installing a formula parser and learning Wilkinson notation to replace three lines of pandas is not a trade that pays off
guide.setupReality: pip install patsy pulls only numpy. Two surprises follow. First, spline functions (bs, cr, cc, te) raise ImportError: spline functionality requires scipy, because scipy is a test-only extra and not a runtime dependency, so you install it yourself. Second, patsy imports the packaging module at import time whenever pandas is importable, and packaging is not in its declared dependencies; in a full data stack something else always pulls it in, but a minimal patsy plus pandas environment fails with ModuleNotFoundError. Beyond that there is no build step, no compiled code, and Python 3.6 and up is claimed. The real cost is learning the formula mini-language and remembering that patsy is in maintenance mode.

alternatives.name: formulaic
alternatives.when: You are writing new code; the patsy maintainers point here as the successor and it is the one still getting features.

alternatives.name: statsmodels
alternatives.when: You want the formulas and the models together; smf.ols and friends call patsy for you and hand back a fitted result.

alternatives.name: scikit-learn
alternatives.when: Your encoding feeds a machine learning pipeline; ColumnTransformer and OneHotEncoder fit, transform, and serialize the sklearn way.

alternatives.name: pandas
alternatives.when: You need dummy columns and nothing else; get_dummies is already imported and there is no formula grammar to learn.

guide.verdict: Still the most convenient way to get an R-style design matrix in Python, and it is unavoidable if you use statsmodels formulas. For new code, take the maintainers at their word and use Formulaic instead.

apiStability.why: The dmatrix and dmatrices signatures have not moved in years and 1.0.0 in November 2024 was mostly a formalization of the existing surface; a frozen project is a stable one.

docsQuality.why: patsy.readthedocs.io has a proper narrative overview, a formula grammar reference, and a page on model prediction with stored DesignInfo; it stops short of covering the scipy requirement for splines or the migration path off patsy.

maintenance.why: The README declares no new feature development since August 2021 and recommends Formulaic; 67 open issues (78 counting PRs) and the 2026 commits are CI and pre-commit bumps rather than fixes.

ecosystem.why: Around 9M weekly downloads and a hard dependency of statsmodels, which keeps it in nearly every Python statistics environment; almost none of that traffic is direct use, and the extension ecosystem never grew.

patterns.title: Turn a formula and a DataFrame into y and X
patterns.snippet:
import pandas as pd
from patsy import dmatrices

df = pd.DataFrame({"y": [1., 2, 3, 4], "x": [1., 2, 3, 4], "g": list("aabb")})

y, X = dmatrices("y ~ x + g", data=df, return_type="dataframe")
print(X.columns.tolist())
# ['Intercept', 'g[T.b]', 'x']
patterns.note: dmatrices splits on the ~ and returns (lhs, rhs). Use dmatrix for the right side only. Without return_type="dataframe" you get a DesignMatrix, which is a numpy ndarray subclass, and you lose the pandas index.

patterns.title: Apply the training encoding to new rows
patterns.snippet:
from patsy import dmatrices, build_design_matrices

y, X = dmatrices("y ~ x + g", data=train_df, return_type="dataframe")
design_info = X.design_info

(X_new,) = build_design_matrices([design_info], new_df, return_type="dataframe")
print(X_new.columns.tolist() == X.columns.tolist())  # True
patterns.note: This is the reason to use patsy at all. Re-running dmatrix on new_df would re-derive category levels and centering means from that data, so a batch missing group 'c' would silently produce a narrower matrix and break your model.

patterns.title: Choose the reference level for a categorical
patterns.snippet:
from patsy import dmatrix, Treatment, Sum

m = dmatrix("C(g, Treatment(reference='b'))", df)
print(m.design_info.column_names)
# ['Intercept', "C(g, Treatment(reference='b'))[T.a]", ...]

dmatrix("C(g, Sum)", df)   # sum-to-zero coding instead
patterns.note: C() also forces a numeric column to be treated as categorical, which matters for integer-coded groups. The [T.x] in a column name means treatment contrast against the omitted reference level; the reference level has no column.

patterns.title: Write interactions and main effects
patterns.snippet:
from patsy import dmatrix

dmatrix("x*g", df).design_info.column_names
# ['Intercept', 'g[T.b]', 'g[T.c]', 'x', 'x:g[T.b]', 'x:g[T.c]']

dmatrix("x:g", df).design_info.column_names
# ['Intercept', 'x:g[a]', 'x:g[b]', 'x:g[c]']
patterns.note: a*b expands to a + b + a:b, while a:b is the interaction alone. Note the encoding changes: with no main effect for g, patsy switches g to full dummy coding to keep the matrix full rank.

patterns.title: Fit without an intercept
patterns.snippet:
from patsy import dmatrix

dmatrix("x - 1", df).design_info.column_names   # ['x']
dmatrix("0 + x", df).design_info.column_names   # ['x']

dmatrix("0 + g", df).design_info.column_names   # ['g[a]', 'g[b]']
patterns.note: - 1 and 0 + are the same thing. Dropping the intercept flips categoricals from treatment coding (k-1 columns) to full dummy coding (k columns), which changes what your coefficients mean.

patterns.title: Transform and escape variables inside the formula
patterns.snippet:
import numpy as np
from patsy import dmatrix

dmatrix("np.log(x)", df)          # any callable in the caller's scope
dmatrix("I(x + 1)", df)           # I() means arithmetic, not formula '+'
dmatrix("Q('total sales')", df)   # Q() quotes an awkward column name
patterns.note: Formula code is evaluated with eval in your calling frame, so np works because you imported it. Without I(), the + is formula syntax and adds a term. Q() is the only way to reference a column with a space or a dash.

patterns.title: Center and standardize with remembered statistics
patterns.snippet:
from patsy import dmatrix, build_design_matrices

train = dmatrix("center(x) + standardize(x)", df)
(scored,) = build_design_matrices([train.design_info], new_df)
# new rows are centered by the TRAINING mean, not their own
patterns.note: center, standardize, and scale are stateful transforms: the statistic is captured during the first pass and stored in design_info. Doing the same with a plain np expression would recompute the mean on every dataset and leak information.

patterns.title: Add a B-spline basis to a continuous term
patterns.snippet:
from patsy import dmatrix

m = dmatrix("bs(x, df=4)", df)   # needs scipy installed
print(m.shape)                   # (n, 5) including the intercept

dmatrix("cr(x, df=4)", df)       # natural cubic regression spline
patterns.note: Splines raise PatsyError wrapping ImportError: spline functionality requires scipy, because scipy is a test extra rather than a runtime dependency. Knot placement is also a stateful transform, so build_design_matrices reuses the training knots.

patterns.title: Control what happens to NaN rows
patterns.snippet:
from patsy import dmatrices, NAAction

y, X = dmatrices("y ~ x", df_with_nan, return_type="dataframe")
print(X.index.tolist())   # NaN rows silently dropped by default

dmatrices("y ~ x", df_with_nan, NA_action=NAAction(on_NA="raise"))
# patsy.PatsyError: factor contains missing values
patterns.note: The default is on_NA="drop", and it drops from both y and X together so they stay aligned. It is silent, so check X.shape against len(df) if row count matters, or pass on_NA="raise" to make the data problem visible.

patterns.title: Map coefficients back to terms
patterns.snippet:
di = dmatrix("x + g", df).design_info

print(di.describe())      # '1 + g + x'
print(di.term_names)      # ['Intercept', 'g', 'x']
print(di.column_names)    # ['Intercept', 'g[T.b]', 'g[T.c]', 'x']
print(di.slice("g"))      # slice(1, 3, None)
patterns.note: One term can span several columns, so di.slice(term) is how you pull all coefficients belonging to a categorical for a joint test. term_names and column_names are different lengths whenever a categorical is present.

patterns.title: Use patsy through statsmodels instead of directly
patterns.snippet:
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

result = smf.ols("y ~ x + C(g)", data=df).fit()
print(result.params.index.tolist())
# ['Intercept', 'C(g)[T.b]', 'x']

result.predict(new_df)   # reuses the stored design_info
patterns.note: This is how almost everyone actually uses patsy. predict() on a fitted result replays the training design_info for you, so unseen category levels raise instead of quietly shifting columns.

patterns.title: Move a formula off patsy
patterns.snippet:
from formulaic import model_matrix

y, X = model_matrix("y ~ x + g", df)
print(X.columns.tolist())      # ['Intercept', 'x', 'g[T.b]']

X_new = X.model_spec.get_model_matrix(new_df)   # the design_info equivalent
patterns.note: Formulaic's ModelSpec plays the role of patsy's DesignInfo. Column names match for common formulas but ordering does not, so anything that indexes coefficients by position needs rechecking after the switch.

guide.whatIs: pause-stream is a classic Node stream that buffers everything written to it while paused and flushes the buffer when you resume. You attach it between a producer you cannot control and a consumer that is not ready yet, call pause(), and no data is lost in between. The important thing to know before you install it: version 0.0.11 has exactly two lines of code. Its index.js reads 'through@2 handles this by default!' followed by module.exports = require('through'). require('pause-stream') and require('through') return the identical function object, verified by strict equality. Everything the package does is done by through 2.3.8, which the package depends on.
useIf: You are maintaining a codebase from the streams1 era that already imports pause-stream and you want to understand what it actually does before touching it
A producer starts emitting before your consumer is wired up and you need a small buffer in between, on old-style Node streams that predate Readable and Writable
You need pause and resume semantics where write() returns false while paused and buffered chunks replay in order on resume, with no object-mode or highWaterMark configuration
Something deep in your dependency tree already pulls it in and you are deciding whether to dedupe it against through rather than remove it
skipIf: You are writing new code: this is streams1 built on the bare Stream class, not Readable or Writable, so it has no _read, no highWaterMark, and no working destroy path for stream.pipeline
You want error propagation: classic .pipe() does not forward errors, and pipeline() cannot clean this stream up properly, so a failure downstream leaves the buffer and the source alive
Memory matters under load: the buffer is a plain array with no size limit, so a paused stream in front of a fast producer grows until the process runs out of heap

You could just depend on through instead, which is the same code with 46 million weekly downloads against this wrapper's 6.1 million, one less package, and a README that is actually about the code you are running
You need a maintained package: the repo was archived in June 2018, the last publish was version 0.0.11 in September 2013, and the npm maintainer account is a placeholder rather than a named person
You are on modern Node and want PassThrough, which is in core, honors backpressure, works with pipeline(), and needs no dependency at all
guide.setupReality: Installation is npm install pause-stream and nothing else: one dependency on through ~2.3, no native build, no config. The real setup surprise is that there is nothing to set up because there is nothing here. Reading index.js takes five seconds and settles the question: the module body is a comment and a re-export of through. So every question you have about pause-stream is really a question about through 2.3.8, and the pause-stream README is a 2013 document describing behavior that lives in a different package. Practical consequences follow from that.
